name: Hyponatraemia and SIADH
aliases: syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: Hyponatraemia is the most common electrolyte disturbance in hospitalised patients and reflects a relative excess of water compared with sodium, usually driven by impaired water excretion
The diagnostic approach begins by confirming true hypotonic hyponatraemia, then assessing volume status and measuring urine osmolality and urine sodium
SIADH is a euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine, elevated urine sodium, and normal thyroid and adrenal function, diagnosed after excluding other causes
Common triggers of SIADH include malignancy, pulmonary disease, central nervous system disorders, and numerous drugs
The severity of symptoms depends more on how quickly sodium falls than on the absolute value, ranging from mild confusion to seizures and cerebral oedema in acute severe cases
The cornerstone of management in SIADH is fluid restriction, with the underlying cause treated wherever possible

Correction must be gradual in chronic hyponatraemia because overly rapid rises in sodium risk osmotic demyelination, whereas acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with severe neurological signs warrants prompt but controlled correction with hypertonic saline
Exclude pseudohyponatraemia and hyperglycaemia-related dilution before attributing a low sodium to a water-handling disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Hyponatraemia develops when water intake exceeds the kidney's ability to excrete free water, diluting plasma sodium. Antidiuretic hormone is central: when its release is appropriate (as in volume depletion or reduced effective circulating volume in heart failure and cirrhosis) or inappropriate (as in SIADH), water is retained and urine remains concentrated. In SIADH, ADH is secreted or acts independently of osmotic and volume signals, so the kidney retains water despite plasma hypotonicity; patients are clinically euvolaemic because the retained water distributes across body compartments and mild volume expansion promotes natriuresis. The fall in plasma osmolality drives water into brain cells, and the resulting cerebral oedema accounts for the neurological features. In chronic hyponatraemia the brain adapts by extruding solutes, which is why rapid correction can dehydrate neurons and cause osmotic demyelination.
additionalDifferentials: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia from renal or extrarenal sodium loss
Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia in heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Plasma osmolality to confirm true hypotonic hyponatraemia
Urine osmolality and urine sodium to assess water handling and volume status
Thyroid function and assessment of adrenal function
Careful clinical evaluation of volume status
Review of medications that can cause hyponatraemia
Investigation for underlying malignancy, pulmonary, or central nervous system disease when SIADH is suspected
redFlags: Seizures, marked confusion, or reduced consciousness indicating severe or acute hyponatraemia
Rapid onset of symptoms suggesting acute cerebral oedema
Overly rapid correction risking osmotic demyelination
reference.prognosis: Mild chronic hyponatraemia is often well tolerated but is associated with falls, cognitive impairment, and worse outcomes in the underlying illness. Acute severe hyponatraemia can be life-threatening from cerebral oedema, while inappropriately rapid correction can cause devastating osmotic demyelination. With cause-directed treatment and appropriately paced correction most patients recover, and SIADH prognosis largely follows that of its underlying cause.
pitfalls: Correcting chronic hyponatraemia too quickly and precipitating osmotic demyelination
Diagnosing SIADH without excluding hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and volume depletion
Giving isotonic saline in SIADH, which can paradoxically worsen the sodium
Overlooking a drug or occult malignancy as the driver of persistent SIADH
management: Treat the underlying trigger of SIADH, such as malignancy, pulmonary or central nervous system disease, or an offending drug, wherever it can be identified and reversed
Make fluid restriction the cornerstone of chronic SIADH management
Treat acute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or marked confusion using hypertonic saline, raising the sodium in a slow, controlled manner
Strictly limit the rate of sodium rise to avoid osmotic demyelination, re-lowering with hypotonic fluid or desmopressin if correction overshoots
Use second-line agents for persistent hyponatraemia, such as oral urea, vasopressin receptor antagonists or demeclocycline
Review and stop medications that provoke hyponatraemia
Monitor serum sodium frequently during correction, having first confirmed true hypotonic, euvolaemic hyponatraemia
Involve nephrology or endocrinology for refractory or diagnostically uncertain cases
